mcqs.question: Why does a fair coin (p=0.5) have higher entropy than a coin biased 90/10?
options: Entropy measures the number of possible outcomes, and both coins have exactly 2
The biased coin has higher entropy because 0.9 is a larger number than 0.5
Entropy is maximized when outcomes are equally likely — a fair coin's outcome is hardest to predict, so it carries the most average surprise
Entropy doesn't depend on probability at all, only on the number of flips
mcqs.explanation: Entropy is the expected surprise (self-information) across outcomes, and it's maximized exactly when a distribution is uniform — you have the least ability to guess the outcome in advance. A biased coin lets you guess 'heads' correctly most of the time, so each flip carries less genuine new information on average, giving lower entropy despite having the same 2 possible outcomes.

mcqs.question: You compute mutual information I(X;Y) = 0 for two features X and Y in your dataset. What does this tell you?
options: X and Y are perfectly correlated
X and Y are independent — knowing the value of one gives you zero information about the other
X and Y must both have zero entropy individually
The dataset has a bug, since mutual information should never equal exactly zero
mcqs.explanation: Mutual information of exactly zero is the defining condition for statistical independence between two variables — learning one tells you literally nothing about the other's distribution. This is the opposite of correlation (option A), and doesn't imply anything about each variable's individual entropy, nor is it a sign of a data bug — many genuinely independent feature pairs exist in real datasets.

mcqs.question: You compute D_KL(p||q) and D_KL(q||p) for the same two distributions p and q. What should you expect?
options: They will always be equal, since KL divergence is a symmetric distance metric
They are equal only when p and q are both Gaussian distributions
Only D_KL(p||q) is mathematically valid; the reverse direction is undefined
They can differ — KL divergence is not symmetric, so the direction you compute it in matters
mcqs.explanation: KL divergence is explicitly not a true distance metric because it lacks symmetry — D_KL(p||q) and D_KL(q||p) are generally different values, each penalizing a different kind of mismatch between the distributions. Both directions are perfectly well-defined mathematically (as long as q is nonzero wherever p is nonzero); this isn't specific to Gaussian distributions.

mcqs.question: In the weather/umbrella example, I(Rain;Umbrella) comes out to about 0.18 bits — small but positive. What does that small positive value actually mean?
options: Umbrella use carries a little genuine signal about rain, but far from perfect — the two aren't independent, though they aren't tightly coupled either
The calculation must have an error, since mutual information for real-world variables should round to either 0 or H(Rain)
Umbrella use and rain are independent, and 0.18 is just rounding noise
0.18 bits means you can predict rain with 18% accuracy from umbrella use alone
mcqs.explanation: A small positive mutual information sits on a continuum between 0 (independence) and H(Rain) (umbrella perfectly determines rain) — it quantifies a real but partial statistical dependence, exactly what you'd expect since people carry umbrellas for reasons besides rain. It isn't a rounding artifact, isn't an accuracy percentage (mutual information is measured in bits, not accuracy), and a nonzero value is a completely normal, error-free result for correlated-but-imperfect real-world signals.
